title: Burst warmup & micro-priming — proto notes
content:
Context:
- Observed problem: customers with bursty traffic patterns (e.g., sudden spikes from scheduled batch jobs, product launches, or weekly reports) hit cold-path latency and penalty on first N tokens while dedicated pools spin up or model variants warm caches.
- This hurts UX and increases SLO error budgets. Existing autoscale + cold-cache tends to be either too slow or too expensive when over-provisioned.

Goal / high-level hypothesis:
- Provide a lightweight, low-cost "micro-warmup" layer that pre-warms model execution state and KV caches for a small set of anticipated prompt prefixes and tenant-specific hot contexts so the first 100–500 tokens have latency comparable to a warmed replica.
- Micro-warmup should be: per-tenant, inexpensive (fractional GPU work / short CPU prefetch), configurable by policy, and safe for private/dedicated/hosted deployments.

Why this would help:
- Reduces p95/p99 for first-response latency on bursts without full reserved capacity.
- Lets Dedicated/Private customers operate with tighter reserved commitments.
- Better unit economics than long-lived overprovisioning.

Constraints and non-goals:
- Not trying to replace full instance warm pools or long-running reserved GPU replicas.
- Should not retain user PII in caches beyond agreed retention. Must respect redaction/KMS policies.
- Latency-sensitive: warmup work must not delay ongoing serving requests (prefer async prefetch).

Key components (brainstorm):
1) Burst predictor & intent hints
   - Simple heuristic hooks: scheduled cron triggers, API header hints (x-redwood-warmup: expected), telemetry-based prediction (sudden ramp detection).
   - CLI / console toggle for customers to register high-confidence prefixes (e.g., system prompts, frequently-used opening lines).

2) Micro-priming cache store
   - Fast in-memory KV for prefix activations (small KV caches of decoder keys). Evict aggressively.
   - Store short serialized activation snapshots (quantized) that can be applied to new requests.
   - TTL and per-tenant quotas.

3) Lightweight warmup runners
   - CPU-bound prefetch for tokenizers, embeddings; GPU micro-shots for short sequence runs (<= 32 tokens) to populate KV.
   - Run in lower-priority preemptible workers to avoid interfering with production inference.

4) Orchestration & fallback
   - Warmup applied only if signature compatible (model, quantization profile, sequence length bucket).
   - Fallback to normal cold path when mismatch.

User stories (rough):
- As a Growth PM, I want my scheduled campaign bursts to have consistent first-response latency so the landing feature feels fast.
- As a Platform SRE, I want per-tenant warmup budgets and visibility so warmups can't starve serving capacity.
- As an Enterprise customer using Private, I want on-prem micro-warmup that honors local KMS and does not send raw prompts off-network.

API / UX sketch (console + header pattern):
- Console: "Burst warmups" page where a user can: register prefixes, set frequency windows, set max warmup budget per hour, enable prediction signals.
- REST: POST /v1/warmup-sessions { model, prefix_hash, tenant_id, ttl_seconds, expected_start_window }
- Header hint: X-RW-WARMUP: true / session-id / prefix-hash

Experiment ideas (MVP):
- Pilot with 3 customers using hosted API. Instrument p95/p99 for first 30s after scheduled spike vs baseline.
- Two warmup modes: "snapshot apply" (restore KV snapshot) vs "micro-shot" (run prefix through model). Compare costs and latency gains.

Success metrics:
- p99-first-token latency drop >= 40% for targeted bursts.
- Warmup cost <= 5% of the additional cost of naive overprovisioning.
- No increase in error rates or privacy violations.

Operational concerns / safety:
- Must ensure warmup work is throttled and accounted to tenant billing (or free trial credits).
- Snapshot format must be signed and versioned; incompatible snapshots should be rejected.
- Security review: ensure KV snapshots do not leak sensitive tokens or secrets. Integrate with redaction and KMS pipeline.

Open questions / unknowns:
- How effective are tiny KV snapshots across quantization variants (8-bit/4-bit)? Do we need separate snapshot classes per quant profile?
- Cost model: GPU micro-shots vs CPU prefetch + local recompile cost. Is it cheaper to run 10 micro-shots than to keep one extra warm replica for 5 minutes?
- Does warmup introduce variance for subsequent concurrent requests that expect cold behavior (cache priming affecting determinism)?

Risks / failure modes:
- Warmup runaway: misconfigured prediction could cause sustained background warmups, consuming capacity. Mitigate with hard quotas and ex post audits.
- Snapshot staleness: model rollout invalidates snapshots and increases errors. Need eviction on model version change and rollout integration.

Next steps (practical):
- Spike #1: implement minimal snapshot apply for one small open model (Llama2-7b-ish) on a dev pool, test retrieving snapshot and applying to cold request path. Measure delta for first 100 tokens. Owner: Jun. ETA: 2 weeks.
- Spike #2: micro-shot runner on preemptible GPU, run short prefix (<= 16 tokens) to populate KV, measure cost and prep time. Owner: Sam. ETA: 2 weeks (parallel).
- Product: draft console wireframe and quota model for customers. Owner: Ava. ETA: 1 week.
- Create Jira ticket JIRA-RT-412 to track integration with rollouts and billing.

Notes-to-self:
- Keep warmup TTL short (30–300s) to avoid stale contexts.
- Investigate whether Combine with caching of deterministic embeddings for prompt prefixes to reduce the need for GPU micro-shots.
- Talk to security about snapshot retention policy before demo to any enterprise customer.
- Add a "dry-run" mode where warmup runs but cost is not billed so we can A/B test.

References / similar thinking from drive: cost-sim sandbox, token-batching hierarchy notes, microcapacity surfacing experiments — pull those fetches into the spike plan.

End of notes (rough). Will iterate after Spike results.
